## Failure mode

**What it produces.** A flipped y-axis produces a tissue map that is anatomically plausible and entirely mirrored. Nothing errors.

**The diagnostic that catches it.** Overlay on the image with an asymmetric landmark visible; the mirror is obvious only then.

## Self-check

### Question 1

Is your scale bar in microns or pixels?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Check, do not assume. Read the microns-per-pixel value from the run metadata and confirm your plotted scale bar was drawn from it. If your bar is in pixels, every distance threshold downstream — neighbourhood radii, interaction distances — is scaled by an unknown constant.
:::

### Question 2

Which element defines the extrinsic system?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Whichever element you registered the others into, and it should be a deliberate choice rather than whichever loaded first. In SpatialData that is the coordinate system named in the transformation; ask which element defines it and what the transformation to it actually is. If the answer is identity for everything, nobody registered anything.
:::

### Question 3

What does the overlay look like if you skip the transform?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Often, entirely reasonable — which is the problem. Points and image may span similar numeric ranges by coincidence, so the overlay looks plausible while being offset or mirrored. That is why the check requires an asymmetric landmark: with a symmetric field of view, skipping the transform and applying it correctly can produce indistinguishable pictures.
:::
